evidence.title: Experimental investigation of real-time 3D beam's eye view image-guided radiotherapy for prostate SBRT

evidence.effect: 46 failure modes identified; mitigation reduced RPN by an average of 43% across top ten high-risk failure modes.

commentary.bottom_line: Four offline or simulated studies suggest that structured multidisciplinary hazard analysis can identify dozens of application-specific failure modes, and two report lower risk ratings after mitigation. No study measured whether this practice reduces harm to patients, so the evidence for R052 rests on process outcomes.

perspectives.view: Four studies test the practice, all at evidence level 4 and all offline or simulated. Three apply multidisciplinary FMEA or fault tree analysis to AI workflows, one of them in radiotherapy. One randomized study tests AI-generated stories as prompts for harm identification. None measures patient outcomes, so indirectness and small samples leave certainty very low.

A Belgian FMEA of an AI planning workflow identified 39 failure modes. One was rated Not acceptable before mitigation, and none were after. A second team found 46 failure modes and reported an average 43% RPN reduction across the top ten. The process may surface and reprioritize risks, but RPN values are expert ratings, and no study counted errors reaching patients.

In a Chinese AI-driven radiotherapy workflow, eight experts identified 86 failure modes across 5 steps and 28 sub-steps. Of these, 25 were high risk, mostly in ROI delineation, and human error was the primary factor. This suggests that many hazards may arise where staff interact with the tool rather than in the model alone.

FDA draft guidance expects manufacturers to identify hazards under normal and fault conditions. Utah HB 452 requires identification of foreseeable adverse outcomes for mental health chatbots. The tested studies examined clinical AI workflows and a harm-elicitation exercise. None was described as evaluating a mental health chatbot, so evidence for that statutory setting is indirect.

The tested exercises relied on multidisciplinary expert panels, including one of eight experts, and none reported staff hours or costs. CHAI's guide notes that use-specific testing may burden clinicians. Leaders may need a staffing commitment for each tool reviewed, but the studies do not measure its size.

In a randomized study, participants without AI-generated stories directed 79.1% of responses to privacy and well-being. Those who read stories spread responses across all 17 harm types. This may mean that unaided review teams overlook some harms that matter to patients. Patients receiving care were not the subjects of the study.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI deployments with and without structured multidisciplinary hazard analysis on errors that reach patients or on adverse events. The existing tests are offline or simulated and cover a small number of clinical workflows. Prospective evaluations in other clinical domains, including patient-facing chatbots and generative AI tools, should report detection of real-world failures and the staff time and cost of the process.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the four tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. All were offline exercises in Belgium, China, or an unreported setting. It remains unknown whether hazard teams identify failure modes specific to these groups, such as language or comprehension errors, unless members who represent them take part in the review.
